title: API Design: REST & GraphQL
requirement: Experience designing, building, maintaining RESTful and GraphQL APIs.

questions.question: What are the core constraints that make an API RESTful?
questions.answer: REST means resources, standard HTTP verbs used with their real semantics, and representations like JSON. It's stateless, so scaling is horizontal, and it's cacheable. In practice I care more about good resource modeling and correct status codes than purism.
questions.keyTakeaway: Model resources, not actions; let HTTP verbs and status codes carry meaning.

questions.question: What problem does GraphQL solve compared with REST, and what does the diagram show?
questions.answer: REST returns fixed shapes, so clients over-fetch or call several endpoints per view. GraphQL lets the client ask for exact fields in one round trip. The trade-off is that complexity moves to the server: caching, cost control, and N+1 become your problem.
questions.keyTakeaway: GraphQL trades server complexity for exactly-shaped, single-request responses.

questions.question: How do you decide between REST and GraphQL for a new public API?
questions.answer: I default to REST for public APIs because you get HTTP caching, CDNs, and per-endpoint rate limiting. I pick GraphQL when client needs vary a lot or I'm aggregating many services, and then I add persisted queries, depth limits, and batching.
questions.keyTakeaway: REST for public cacheable resources; GraphQL for diverse clients over a nested graph.

questions.question: How do you evolve an API without breaking existing clients?
questions.answer: I default to additive changes. New optional fields and endpoints don't break anything if clients ignore unknown fields. For real breaks I version, publish a deprecation timeline, and watch old-version usage before retiring it.
questions.keyTakeaway: Evolve additively; version only for real breaks, with a published sunset.

questions.question: What is the N+1 problem in GraphQL and how do you fix it?
questions.answer: A resolver that fetches per field runs one query per related object, so 50 orders with an author field fire 51 calls. The fix is batching: collect the keys within a request and load them in one query. I use DataLoader, then confirm with tracing that the call count is constant.
questions.keyTakeaway: Batch field loads per request with DataLoader; N+1 calls become one.

questions.question: Which HTTP methods are safe and idempotent, and why does it matter for clients?
questions.answer: GET and HEAD are safe, so caches may repeat them. PUT and DELETE are idempotent, so retries are fine. POST is neither, so a retry can double-create unless the server dedupes with an idempotency key.
questions.keyTakeaway: Safe methods never change state; idempotent methods are retry-safe; POST needs a key.

questions.question: How do you design pagination for a large, changing collection?
questions.answer: I use cursor pagination. An opaque cursor encodes the sort key and last item's id, and the next page starts after it. Offsets skip or repeat rows when data changes, and they still scan skipped rows. Keyset indexes keep latency flat.
questions.keyTakeaway: Cursor pagination stays correct under writes and fast at depth; offsets do not.

questions.question: How do you protect an API, especially GraphQL, from abusive or expensive queries?
questions.answer: I authenticate at the edge and authorize per resource, not just per endpoint. Rate limits go per identity. For GraphQL I add depth limits, complexity budgets, and persisted queries.
questions.keyTakeaway: Limit depth, cost, and introspection; authorize per resource, per identity.

rows.label: Rate limits
rows.note: Per identity, not just per IP

questions.question: How do you design a rate limiter, and which algorithm fits which case?
questions.answer: I enforce limits server-side, in middleware or the gateway, and return 429 with Retry-After. My default is a token bucket: it refills at a fixed rate into a bounded capacity, so it's cheap and tolerates bursts. Sliding window counters avoid the fixed-window edge, where a burst across the boundary doubles the limit. In a cluster I update shared counters atomically so nodes can't over-admit.
questions.keyTakeaway: Token bucket by default, sliding window against edge bursts, atomic shared counters.

questions.question: How do you design webhooks so consumers can trust and reliably process them?
questions.answer: I treat webhooks as an API I expose. I sign an HMAC over the timestamp plus the raw body with a per-endpoint secret, so receivers can verify it and reject replays. Each event has a unique id for dedupe, and I never promise ordering. I retry non-2xx with exponential backoff and dead-letter failures.
questions.keyTakeaway: Sign payloads with HMAC, dedupe by event id, and never promise ordering.

questions.question: How do you expose an operation that takes minutes without holding the HTTP request open?
questions.answer: I never hold an HTTP request open for minutes. I return 202 Accepted with a Location header pointing at an operation resource with states like queued, running, succeeded, and failed. I default to polling, since it's stateless, and use SSE only when progress visibility matters.
questions.keyTakeaway: Return 202 with a pollable operation resource; reserve push for real progress needs.

questions.question: How do conditional requests with ETags work, and why should every API support them?
questions.answer: The server stamps each representation with an ETag. The client sends it back as If-None-Match, and if nothing changed it gets a 304 with no body. Requiring If-Match on writes also gives optimistic concurrency, so lost updates become a clean 412. It's the cheapest performance win in HTTP API design.
questions.keyTakeaway: ETags with If-None-Match turn refetches into 304s that carry no body.

code.snippet:
curl -s -D - -o /dev/null https://api.example.com/orders/42 \
  -H 'If-None-Match: "7c9e6"'
# 304 Not Modified: empty body, cache stays valid
# 200: changed; response carries the new ETag to store

questions.question: How do you design a bulk endpoint that handles partial failures honestly?
questions.answer: Twenty POSTs waste round trips and multiply retry logic. I'd offer a bulk endpoint that takes an array and returns one result per item: ids for successes, and structured errors with the item's index for failures, as a 207 or a 200 with a results array. I fail the whole batch only when the business needs atomicity, and I cap batch size.
questions.keyTakeaway: Bulk endpoints report per-item outcomes; partial success beats all-or-nothing failure.

questions.question: How do you standardize error responses across a large API surface?
questions.answer: I pick one error format and enforce it everywhere. My default is RFC 9457 problem details because it's a standard. Every failure returns a type URI, title, status, and detail, and clients switch on the type URI. Mixed 400 shapes force defensive parsing in every consumer.
questions.keyTakeaway: Return RFC 9457 problem+json with a type URI on every failure.

rows.label: type
rows.note: URI for the error class, clients switch on it

questions.question: What is the backend-for-frontend pattern, and where do teams misuse it?
questions.answer: A backend-for-frontend gives each client family its own aggregation layer, owned by that client's team. The gateway keeps cross-cutting concerns. I avoid one unified aggregation API, because every feature changes it. BFFs stay thin, with shared logic in a domain service.
questions.keyTakeaway: Give each client family a thin BFF; gateways stay cross-cutting, BFFs stay logic-free.

questions.question: How do you choose between schema-first and code-first API development?
questions.answer: Schema-first means the contract, whether OpenAPI, protobuf, or GraphQL SDL, is reviewed before implementation. For public and cross-team APIs I go schema-first, which gives real review, parallel client work, and honest SDKs. Code-first is faster internally, but the spec drifts unless CI diffs it on every merge.
questions.keyTakeaway: Schema-first for shared contracts; code-first only with CI spec diffing.

questions.question: When do you pick SSE versus WebSockets versus polling for live updates?
questions.answer: I match the transport to the direction and freshness I need. Polling works when minutes-old data is fine. SSE gives one-way push over plain HTTP with automatic reconnection, which suits notifications and progress bars. I use WebSockets only when the client streams data back continuously, like chat or collaborative editing.
questions.keyTakeaway: Poll for tolerant clients, SSE for one-way push, WebSockets only for true bidirectionality.

questions.question: How do you combine pagination with filtering and sorting without wrecking performance?
questions.answer: I design filtering, sorting, and pagination as one contract. First I fix a stable total order, with a unique tiebreaker like id backed by an index, because cursors are only as stable as that order. Filters apply before pagination and must hit indexed predicates. Counts go behind an explicit parameter.
questions.keyTakeaway: Pin a unique, indexed sort order first; filters run before pagination, counts behind a flag.

diagram.title: Filter, sort and paginate as one contract

questions.question: How do you implement idempotency keys correctly on the server?
questions.answer: I store the outcome in Redis or a database, keyed by the Idempotency-Key header scoped to client and route. A completed key returns the saved response, an in-flight key returns 409, and the same key with a different body returns 422.
questions.keyTakeaway: Persist key, status, and full response; replays return the saved result, mismatches get 422.

questions.question: What does good API design look like with gRPC, and how do you evolve protobuf contracts?
questions.answer: gRPC gives a strict protobuf contract, HTTP/2 framing, and generated clients, so it fits internal service traffic. I never reuse or renumber field tags, I reserve the numbers of deleted fields, and I only add optional fields, because anything else breaks the wire format silently. I version through the package path, like payments.v1.
questions.keyTakeaway: In protobuf, reserve retired field numbers, add only optional fields, version via package path.

questions.question: How do you run deprecation and sunset for old API versions in practice?
questions.answer: I treat deprecation as a program with dates, not a changelog note. Old versions carry Deprecation and Sunset headers, and I track which clients still call them, since 'we think nobody uses it' causes outages. I retire only once usage is below an agreed threshold, with a grace period.
questions.keyTakeaway: Deprecate with Sunset headers, measured usage, and a reversible shutdown date.

questions.question: How does multi-tenancy change API design?
questions.answer: I resolve the tenant at the edge, from subdomain, token claim, or header, and pass it as explicit context through every layer, because implicit tenancy eventually crosses tenants. I enforce isolation in the data layer, with Postgres row-level security as the cheap option. I also rate-limit and meter per tenant.
questions.keyTakeaway: Resolve tenancy at the edge, enforce it in the data layer, meter per tenant.

questions.question: Is HATEOAS worth implementing, or is it REST purity theater?
questions.answer: Full HATEOAS stays rare because tooling and consumers prefer contracts. My middle ground is to embed links only for things that genuinely vary, like a next-page link or a payment redirect. When the server controls the flow, links let you change steps without breaking clients.
questions.keyTakeaway: Use hypermedia links for server-driven flows; skip full HATEOAS for contract-first docs.

questions.question: How do you prevent lost updates when many clients write the same resource?
questions.answer: When two clients read then write the same resource, last-write-wins silently deletes work. I require conditional writes: the client sends If-Match with the ETag it read, and the server answers 412 Precondition Failed with the current resource if the state has moved. The client reapplies and retries. I use locking only for hot resources like seat inventory.
questions.keyTakeaway: Require If-Match conditional writes and answer mismatches with 412 plus current state.

questions.question: How do consumer-driven contract tests change how you ship API changes safely?
questions.answer: Consumer-driven contract tests catch the breaks that page you, like a consumer depending on a renamed field. The consumer writes a contract of what it calls and expects, and publishes it. The provider verifies every contract in CI, so a breaking change fails the build before merge.
questions.keyTakeaway: Consumer-defined contracts verified against the provider in CI catch breaks before merge.

questions.question: How do you choose between JSON Merge Patch and JSON Patch for partial updates?
questions.answer: JSON Merge Patch, RFC 7386, is an object of fields to change where null deletes a field. It's simple, but it can't update array elements. JSON Patch, RFC 6902, is a list of add, remove, replace, and move operations, precise for arrays but hard to hand-author. I use merge-patch for simple resources and JSON Patch for arrays or atomic edits.
questions.keyTakeaway: Merge Patch for simple field updates; JSON Patch when arrays or atomic edits matter.

questions.question: How do you evolve a GraphQL schema when URL versioning is not an option?
questions.answer: GraphQL doesn't version by URL, so the schema evolves in place. I add nullable fields only, and retire a field with @deprecated and a reason naming the replacement. I never delete it while anyone still calls it, and persisted queries show who does. CI fails on breaking schema diffs.
questions.keyTakeaway: Evolve GraphQL in place: nullable additions, @deprecated retirements, CI schema diffs.
